text: Urbanization, Technological Progress, and Economic History Joel Mokyr It has become customary among economic historians to distin­ guish four different sources of economic growth (see, for example, Mokyr, 1990, for an exposition).

Economic History 
Joel Mokyr 
It has become customary among economic historians to distin­
guish four different sources of economic growth (see, for example, 
Mokyr, 1990, for an exposition).

The topic of agglomeration economies and diseconomies has kept 
urban economists busy for more than a generation.

text: Most of the satisfying work has been at the theoretical level; although there has been some interesting empirical research, a thoroughly con­ vincing analysis remains elusive.

Most of the 
satisfying work has been at the theoretical level; although there 
has been some interesting empirical research, a thoroughly con­
vincing analysis remains elusive.

text: As the relative amount of space devoted to them in this paper implies, I find the more promising areas of research are (i) the links between agglomeration econ­ omies/congestion costs and changes in metropolitan spatial structure, and (ii) the debate about the possible elimination of agglomeration economies.
text_raw:
As the relative amount of space 
devoted to them in this paper implies, I find the more promising 
areas of research are (i) the links between agglomeration econ­
omies/congestion costs and changes in metropolitan spatial 
structure, and (ii) the debate about the possible elimination of 
agglomeration economies.

text: Much remains to be done, particularly because of the divorce between the theoretical research and the empirical studies.

because of the divorce between the theoretical research and the

text: The basic determinant has been the general shift from industrial activities to service activities in the whole economy, a shift that was driven mainly by sectorally different income elasticities of demand and the disappearance of the pro­ ductivity bias between manufacturing and services.
text_raw:
The basic determinant has been the general 
shift from industrial activities to service activities in the whole 
economy, a shift that was driven mainly by sectorally different 
income elasticities of demand and the disappearance of the pro­
ductivity bias between manufacturing and services.

text: Without loea­ tional shifts of producers, this general trend would have resulted in higher growth rates of service-intensive urban areas.
text_raw:
Without loea­
tional shifts of producers, this general trend would have resulted 
in higher growth rates of service-intensive urban areas.

text: It was overcompensated, however, by the increased regional mobility of service producers.
text_raw:
It was 
overcompensated, however, by the increased regional mobility of 
service producers.

text: Presumably, this second determinant mainly reflects the enriched technological opportunities for providing dis­ embodied services across long distances and for the disembodi­ ment of embodied services.
text_raw:
Presumably, this second determinant mainly 
reflects the enriched technological opportunities for providing dis­
embodied services across long distances and for the disembodi­
ment of embodied services.

text: As structural change towards services is ongoing and technical progress in information and communica­ tions technologies is still very rapid, it can be expected that the growth potential of rural areas will be more promising than that of urban areas also in the years to come.
text_raw:
As structural change towards services 
is ongoing and technical progress in information and communica­
tions technologies is still very rapid, it can be expected that the 
growth potential of rural areas will be more promising than that 
of urban areas also in the years to come.

text: Although the emphasis of this paper does not lie on policy aspects, it is tempting to draw some conclusions that appear to be important for the design of regional policies.
text_raw:
Although the emphasis of this paper does not lie on policy 
aspects, it is tempting to draw some conclusions that appear to be 
important for the design of regional policies.

text: First of all, regional policymakers should take into account that the most dynami~ industries in highly developed economies are to be found in the service sector.
text_raw:
First of all, regional policymakers should take into account 
that the most dynami~ industries in highly developed economies 
are to be found in the service sector.

text: Despite this well-known fact, the regional policies of most countries or the Ee are still primarily concerned with attracting manufacturing activities to backward regions.
text_raw:
Despite this well-known fact, 
the regional policies of most countries or the Ee are still primarily 
concerned with attracting manufacturing activities to backward 
regions.

text: This priority seems to be increasingly misplaced.
text_raw: This priority seems to be increasingly misplaced.

text: It prob­ ably reflects the vague intuition of many observers that economic prosperity rests basically upon a flourishing industrial sector and that service activities are not much more than an addendum that would be unable to survive without a solid industrial base.
text_raw:
It prob­
ably reflects the vague intuition of many observers that economic 
prosperity rests basically upon a flourishing industrial sector and 
that service activities are not much more than an addendum that 
would be unable to survive without a solid industrial base.

text: This view was already expressed by Kaldor (1966), who argued that the high share of services was the main reason for the slow growth of the British economy, or by Baumol (1967), who blamed the poor productivity performance of services for causing urban crisis.
text_raw:
This view was already expressed by Kaldor (1966), who argued 
that the high share of services was the main reason for the slow 
growth of the British economy, or by Baumol (1967), who blamed 
the poor productivity performance of services for causing urban 
crisis.

text: In recent years, it has turned up in the debate about the alleged dangers of deindustrialization in the United States and in Europe as well (see, e.g., Bluestone and Harrison, 1982;
Rowthorn and Wells, 1987;

and Wells, 1987;

services to those regions where the corresponding demand is miss­
ing.

text: The prospects of using regienal policy instruments to change the locational decisions of producers of disembodied services, on the other hand, are much better because these producers can take advantage of rich opportunities as concerns bridging long dis­ tances to their customers and are able to react to incentives pro­ vided by regional policies.

The prospects of using regienal policy instruments to change 
the locational decisions of producers of disembodied services, on 
the other hand, are much better because these producers can take 
advantage of rich opportunities as concerns bridging long dis­
tances to their customers and are able to react to incentives pro­

text: Within the category of disembodied services, however, one must distinguish between urban and footloose services.
text_raw:
Within the category of disembodied services, however, one 
must distinguish between urban and footloose services.

text: Urban services depend heavily on network externalities that require a certain amount of agglomeration and regional clustering.
text_raw:

services depend heavily on network externalities that require a

therefore, that their influence on the localization of urban services 
is rather limited.

text: Congestion pricing has many losers, making it more difficult, though perhaps not impos­ sible, to design a package of revenue uses that is understandable, credible, and capable of offsetting the losses for most groups of citizens.

sible, to design a package of revenue uses that is understandable, 
credible, and capable of offsetting the losses for most groups of 
citizens.

text: The politics of pricing policies have recently been more en­ couraging, but it is still unlikely that they will be adopted soon in any thing, like a full-scale application.

text: So what is there in the meantime?

text: There are some modest policies that can make a modest differ­ ence.

ence.

text: High-occu­ pancy vehicle lanes can offer carpools and busses a premium ser­ vice, saving them time and money and improving the patronage and financial viability of bus transit.

pancy vehicle lanes can offer carpools and busses a premium ser­
vice, saving them time and money and improving the patronage

text: Such lanes may also provide a limited niche for introducing congestion pricing, by offering solo drivers the option of using these faster lanes for a fee, as is being planned for two freeways in southern California (Fielding and Klein, 1993).
